entries.topic: The Bank of England and the national debt, 1672–1815

claims.text: On 2 January 1672 Charles II's government began the 'Stop of the Exchequer', suspending repayment of Exchequer orders and warrants; planned for one year, it was extended to May 1673 and then to January 1674.

The obligations caught by the Stop were later estimated at £1,211,065 (Horsefield); the principal was assessed at £1,328,526 at the end of 1676. Goldsmith-bankers including Edward Backwell and Robert Vyner went bankrupt.

The Bank of England's own museum explains the Bank's founding as a consequence of that default: Charles II's failure to repay the goldsmiths left them unwilling to lend to the Crown, so William III, needing money for war against France, had to find another lender.
The Bank of England was formally established by Royal Charter on 27 July 1694.

William Paterson, a Scottish merchant, proposed that members of the public lend the government £1.2 million (about £200 million today, by the Bank's own estimate); 1,268 subscribers raised it in 11 days.

The government paid the lenders 8% interest; the Bank's museum notes that goldsmiths had typically charged 20 to 30%. The lenders became shareholders in a joint-stock company named 'The Governor and the Company of the Bank of England'.

A reference summary of the national debt's history, citing H. Roseveare's The Financial Revolution 1660–1760 (1991), credits Charles Montagu with devising the Bank's establishment, records a £4,000 yearly management charge on the loan, and names Sir John Houblon as first governor; the charter was granted through the Tonnage Act 1694.

The Bank's 1970 booklet 'The Bank of England: History and Functions' states that the Bank was 'incorporated by Act of Parliament and Charter in 1694' to help 'finance the war being fought by William III against Louis XIV of France', and that it first operated in the Hall of the Mercers' Company in Cheapside.

The same booklet describes the Bank as 'banker to the Government' and manager of 'the Government Stocks which form the bulk of the National Debt'; it dates the centralizing of note issue to the Bank Act of 1844 and public ownership to the Bank of England Act of 1946.
At the end of the Napoleonic Wars British government debt reached a peak of about £1 billion, more than 200% of GDP (figure cited by the reference summary to ukpublicspending.co.uk).

positions.view: The Bank's museum credits the scheme to William Paterson, who proposed that the public lend to the government.

The reference summary, citing Roseveare, credits Charles Montagu with devising the establishment, and notes Paterson's plan had been proposed about three years earlier without being acted on. The two accounts are compatible: Paterson proposed, Montagu carried it through.

entries.topic: Palestine between Napoleon and the Oriental Crisis, 1799–1840

claims.text: During his Egyptian and Syrian campaign Napoleon Bonaparte besieged Acre in 1799; the campaign was defeated by combined British and Ottoman forces.
The French Gazette nationale of 3 Prairial, Year VII (22 May 1799) printed a short report that Bonaparte had invited the Jews of Asia and Africa to gather under his flag.

A fuller text, a 'Letter to the Jewish Nation' headed 'General Headquarters, Jerusalem, 1st Floréal [Year VII], April 20th, 1799' and addressed to the 'rightful heirs of Palestine', was first published in 1940, when Franz Kobler announced a German translation in The New Judaea; no original has been found.
Napoleon never reached Jerusalem; the Jewish Virtual Library account dates his retreat from Acre to 22 May 1799.
Ibrahim Pasha, son of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali, invaded Ottoman Syria on 31 October 1831 and made Haifa his main base from December 1831; Palestine was under Egyptian rule until 1840.

Ibrahim's conscription order of 25 April 1834 required one Muslim man in five, beginning with 200 from Jerusalem, conscripts to serve for life; he also disarmed Nablus and the Hebron district and imposed new taxes, including one on the Muslim administrative class.
The revolt was led from Nablus by Qasim al-Ahmad, with 'Isa Amar leading the Hebron district; the mufti of Jerusalem, Tahir Afandi al-Husayni, acted as mediator and was later exiled.

On 19–20 May 1834 about 36 rebels entered Jerusalem through an abandoned sewer near the Dung Gate and opened it to the rest; the first day's fighting killed 50 peasants, 16 townspeople and five soldiers.

Rood's account, based on Jerusalem Islamic court records, reports that Ibrahim lost 1,500 of 9,000 soldiers in rebel ambushes, that 33 Christian men and women of Bayt Jala were killed on suspicion of looting, and that Hebron was besieged on 24 July, after which 630 young men were sent to Egypt for the army.
Qasim al-Ahmad was captured in Transjordan in August 1834 and beheaded in Damascus; his sons were beheaded in Acre.

A reference summary of the revolt reports that some 10,000 peasants were deported to Egypt and that deportation, conscription and flight reduced Palestine's male population by about one-fifth; it records the rebels' stated aim as expelling the Egyptians and restoring Ottoman rule.
On 15 July 1840, in the Convention of London, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia backed Sultan Abdülmecid I against Muhammad Ali, offering him hereditary rule of Egypt if he withdrew from Syria.

British and allied ships shelled Beirut and Sidon on 11 September 1840 and bombarded Acre on 3 November 1840; Muhammad Ali accepted terms on 27 November 1840, withdrawing from Syria and the Holy Land in return for hereditary rule of Egypt and Sudan.
An analysis of the crisis by William Erich Ellison (2024) states that Britain sought to 'preserve Turkey' as a route to India and a bulwark against Russian expansion.

disputes.question: Did Napoleon issue a proclamation inviting Jews to restore themselves in Palestine?

positions.view: A 1799 newspaper did report an invitation to Jews, but the detailed 1799 letter is a later forgery: Simon Schwarzfuchs (1979), Henry Laurens, Ronald Schechter and Jeremy Popkin regard the German text as forged, and Schechter reads the 1799 report as a rumour. A French Jewish educational site calls the forgery 'almost certainly established' and attributes it to Frankist circles.

Mordechai Gichon argues Napoleon did conceive of a Jewish national home in the Land of Israel; Nathan Schur reads the report as propaganda aimed at local Jews; the Jewish Virtual Library prints the letter and says its authenticity 'has been debated ever since'.

disputes.question: Was the 1834 revolt an early moment of Palestinian national identity?

positions.view: Baruch Kimmerling and Joel Migdal (The Palestinian People, 2003) treat the revolt as formative, because it joined disparate groups against a common enemy who later re-emerged as the Palestinian people.

Benny Morris argues the rebels demanded no independence, likely saw themselves as Ottoman subjects, Arabs or Syrians, and left no lasting national tradition; the reference summary also notes the revolt is largely absent from Palestinian collective memory and that its stated aim was to restore Ottoman rule.

Shimon Shamir sees the Egyptian period as the first application of the territorial state in Palestine; Adel Manna argues 20th-century attitudes to the Ottomans and Muhammad Ali shaped how the revolt was written about.
Rood: Hebron besieged 24 July; 630 young men sent to Egypt.
Reference summary: Hebron defeated 4 August; about 500 killed and 750 men conscripted.

entries.topic: Reform from Istanbul: the Tanzimat edicts and the first Ottoman parliament, 1839–1878

claims.text: The Edict of Gülhane, proclaimed on 3 November 1839 by Sultan Abdülmecid I at the urging of Grand Vizier Mustafa Reşid Pasha, opened the Tanzimat era; it promised security of life, honour and property, a regular tax system in place of tax farming, and regular conscription.
The Gülhane edict stated that its concessions extended 'to all our subjects, whatever religion or sect they may belong to'; it changed no laws by itself and was never fully implemented.

The Reform Edict of 18 February 1856, issued as the Crimean War ended, promised equality in education, government appointments and justice regardless of creed, freedom of worship, and mixed tribunals for cases between Muslims and non-Muslims; military service for non-Muslims was among its unpopular provisions.
The Ottoman constitution was promulgated on 23 December 1876, and the first parliament opened on 19 March 1877 at Dolmabahçe Palace; deputies were chosen indirectly through provincial councils.
Sultan Abdul Hamid II suspended the parliament and the constitution in February 1878 (14 February in one account, 13 February in another).

Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi, born in Jerusalem in 1842, was elected in 1877 as the sole deputy for the Jerusalem mutasarrifate, one of fourteen Arab deputies among 120 by PalQuest's count, and was a prominent opponent of Abdul Hamid II in the chamber.
When the chamber was dissolved in 1878, al-Khalidi was one of ten opposition deputies ordered out of Istanbul.

Al-Khalidi was educated at al-Fakhriyya school, the British Diocesan Boys' School in Jerusalem, a Protestant college in Malta, and in Istanbul; in 1875 The Jewish Chronicle published two of his letters on the Jews of Palestine.

Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin (1878) declared that 'in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person'; British diplomats later cited it against Ottoman restrictions on Jews.

Beyond this chapter: on 1 March 1899 al-Khalidi wrote to Theodor Herzl through Zadok Kahn, Chief Rabbi of France, urging that Palestine be left in peace; Herzl replied on 19 March 1899 that Jewish immigration would benefit the country.

disputes.question: Size of the 1877 Chamber of Deputies

positions.view: 120 deputies, fourteen of them Arab (PalQuest).
115 members (Wikipedia, which also gives a 69 Muslim / 46 non-Muslim split for the second elections).

disputes.question: When was al-Khalidi mayor of Jerusalem?

positions.view: 1870–1874, with two later terms (PalQuest).
Appointed September 1865 at 23 and head of the municipality for nine years (Jerusalem Story).

entries.topic: The 1858 Land Code, the 1867 foreigners' property law, and the estates

claims.text: Ruth Kark (Hebrew University, 2017) treats the 1858 Land Code, the 1858 Tabu (title-deed) Law and an 1867 law allowing foreigners to acquire land as one privatization process that began land survey, registration and mapping in nineteenth-century Palestine.

Kark finds that land came to be concentrated in 'families of urban effendis (absentee landlords)' living in cities in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Palestine, and that effendi ownership made it easier for Jewish immigrants to buy part of this land.
According to Kark, more than 52 estate buildings became the first core of Jewish agricultural settlements, and at least 15 became the core of German Christian settlements or religious institutions.

Article II of the Ottoman law of 1867 on foreigners' real property, as quoted by the US minister at Constantinople, placed foreign landowners 'upon terms of equality with Ottoman subjects in all things that concern their landed property'; the United States accepted it by protocol in 1874.

A Turkish thesis on land ownership by foreigners and Jews in late Ottoman Palestine (Marmara University) calls the 1867 'Safer Kanunu' an attempt to bring foreigners' purchases under legal control, and argues that Jews used gaps in the law to buy fertile, strategic land where the first settlements were later built.

A reference summary records that foreigners were officially barred from buying land in Palestine from 1856 and that the ban held in practice until 1867 (citing Kark 1984); it quotes Yehoshua Porath (1977) that the 1858 code 'brought about the appropriation by the influential and rich families of Beirut, Damascus' and other cities of vast tracts.
The same summary, citing Nasser Abufarha, says cultivators resisted registration because registration brought taxes and conscription.

disputes.question: How to characterize the effect of the 1867 law on Jewish land purchase

positions.view: A legal loophole: Jews exploited gaps in the 1867 law (Marmara thesis).
Part of a wider privatization: the 1858–1867 laws concentrated land in effendi hands, and that concentration made Jewish and German Christian purchases easier (Kark).

entries.topic: Ottoman limits on Jewish immigration and land purchase, 1882–1896, and why they leaked

claims.text: According to Büşra Barın's study of Ottoman policy (METU, 2014), in June 1882 the entry of foreign Jews into Ottoman territory and their purchase of land were forbidden; in July 1882 Jews were allowed to settle anywhere in the empire except Palestine, provided they took Ottoman nationality.

A reference summary records that the Ottomans recognized the new wave by November 1882 and imposed restrictions despite a Sultan's permit of May 1882 (citing Neville Mandel, 1974), and that in 1882 the US minister Lew Wallace was told Jews would be welcome anywhere in the empire except Palestine.

Barın: from 1882 only pilgrims were admitted to Palestine; from 1884 Jewish visitors needed visas from Ottoman consulates in their home countries; pilgrim stays were limited to one month, later extended to three for Jews under foreign protection, whose passports were held against a red permit card.

On 5 March 1887 the British consul in Jerusalem, Noel Temple Moore, reported that foreign Jews were 'only allowed to come on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem for one month', the governor citing poverty, overcrowding of the Jewish quarter and public health; the ambassador, Sir William White, replied on 19 October 1887 that the rule was 'ipso facto null and void' for persons under British protection, citing the Capitulations.

On 28 January 1888 the US minister Oscar Straus reported that the Porte had limited the stay of foreign Jews at Jerusalem to one month and planned to extend it to three; the Grand Vizier cited Easter tensions with Christians and a rumour that Jews meant to re-establish a Jewish kingdom around Jerusalem. The US consul reported that a shipload of Russian Jews had been refused landing at Jaffa about two years earlier.

An Ottoman note of 2 March 1888 admitted foreign Jews only on passports stating a pilgrimage, for at most three months; on 19 May 1888 Straus told the State Department that the United States could not accept passport rules tied to religion, which it called 'utterly repugnant' to the US Constitution. Britain had protested in September 1887.

On 14 June 1893 the Foreign Office instructed its ambassador on petitions from British Jews in Jerusalem against regulations 'Prohibiting Jews from buying & selling real Estate in Palestine', holding that rules aimed at Jews for their religion were inconsistent with Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin.

On 29 July 1893 the US minister reported the Grand Vizier's assurance that earlier restrictions 'had been modified' and that the policy was to prevent 'the alienation of the land to nonresidents' and speculators.

An Ottoman note of 27 March 1894, quoted by the US minister in 1898, forbade Jewish immigrants to acquire real property in Palestine 'for political reasons', for 'the prevention of the permanent establishment in Palestine of Jewish immigrants', applying to native and foreign Jews alike, with purchases allowed on a consular certificate that the buyer was not in a barred class.

Barın: enforcement was undermined by the Capitulations and the protégé system, which let foreign Jews live under European consular protection; Britain had declared in 1847 that its consulates would protect Jews whose own states did not. Despite the bans, more than 50,000 Jews settled.

disputes.question: When did the Ottoman ban on land sales to Jews begin?

positions.view: 1892, applying even to Ottoman Jewish subjects (reference summary citing Ocak 2002 and Porath 1977).
A decree of 1893 for Jewish immigrants in Jerusalem, extended the following April to all Jews (Barın).
The operative text cited by US diplomats is an Ottoman note of 27 March 1894; in July 1893 the Grand Vizier said earlier restrictions had been modified.

disputes.question: When did the red permit card begin?

positions.view: Barın's text describes passports held against a red card but footnotes that the system was implemented from 1900.
The 1887–88 diplomatic record documents one-month and three-month pilgrim limits but does not mention a red card.

entries.topic: The first Arab responses to Jewish settlement, 1882–1896

claims.text: Emanuel Beška (Asian and African Studies, 2007) dates modern Jewish immigration and colonization in Palestine to the 1880s and finds that Arab opposition took time to form; the first reactions came from peasants, then artisans and merchants whose livelihoods were affected.

On 24 June 1891 Arab notables in Jerusalem petitioned the Ottoman Grand Vizier to prohibit Russian Jews from entering Palestine and buying land there (reference timeline citing Neville Mandel, The Arabs and Zionism before World War I).

A 1978 review of Mandel's book in The Detroit Jewish News describes the 1891 action as a protest telegram from Arab leaders in Jerusalem and Jaffa calling for an end to Jewish immigration and land purchase, 'barely a decade after the arrival of the Bilu'im'.

A Jewish Agency historical overview states that in 1891 Arab notables from Jerusalem asked the Ottoman administration to prohibit Jewish immigration and land sales, a request 'repeated time and again'; of the earlier local opposition (sporadic attacks and disputes over land) it says it is 'doubtful whether this opposition had any political connotations'.
Beška finds that Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni, mufti of Jerusalem, followed Jewish immigration 'since the 1880s' and took an active stance against it.

On 15 March 1893 the firm J. Frutiger & Co. complained to the German consul that the Jerusalem governor and a 'Commission for Sale' chaired by al-Husayni were blocking land sales to Jews; the firm said the ban had been 'abolished some time ago', while the mufti held it remained in force under new regulations. On 12 May 1893 the consul complained to his ambassador of a campaign to prompt Muslim petitions for a comprehensive ban.
In 1895 Najib al-Hajj, editor of the Cairo paper Abu al-Hol, accused Jewish colonists of taking Arabs' means of livelihood (cited in a related paper excerpted with Beška's article).
Just after this chapter's period, in 1897, a committee chaired by al-Husayni put land sales to Jews in the Jerusalem district on hold for several years.

positions.view: Largely local and not clearly political: the Jewish Agency overview calls early clashes sporadic and doubts they had 'political connotations'.

Organized and directed at the state from the start: the 1891 petition to the Grand Vizier and the Jerusalem mufti's 1893 campaign over land sales were political acts aimed at Ottoman policy (Mandel as cited; Beška).

entries.topic: The Old Yishuv and the First Aliyah in numbers, 1800–1896

claims.text: Barın estimates that about 5,000 Jews came to Palestine between 1800 and 1840 and roughly 25,000 between 1850 and 1880, and puts the Old Yishuv at about 24,000 in 1880, with 13,900 in Jerusalem.
A reference summary gives, citing Mordecai Elia (1971), a Jewish population of 23,000 in 1880 and 80,000 in 1907.
On 5 April 1870 an Ottoman firman permitted the Alliance Israélite Universelle to establish an agricultural school in Jaffa (copy held by the Israel State Archives, JM-ISA/AEB/83/32).

The First Aliyah is dated 1881–1903. Petah Tikva was re-established in 1882 after a first attempt in 1878; Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya'akov and Rosh Pinna (which took over Gei Oni, founded 1878) date from 1882, Ness Ziona from 1883, Gedera from 1884, Rehovot from 1890 and Hadera from 1891.
In 1883 the settlers' central committee transferred Zikhron Ya'akov's assets to Baron Edmond de Rothschild.
Emigration from Yemen began in early 1881; a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby towns for Palestine in 1881–82, part of a movement that continued almost without break until 1914.

In the 1880s the Orthodox community of Jerusalem regarded emerging Zionism as a threat and reported Zionist newcomers to the Ottoman authorities (Sobel and Beit-Hallahmi, eds., Tradition, Innovation, Conflict, 2012, as cited).
Vienna's preacher Adolf Jellinek answered Pinsker's Auto-Emancipation that Jews had no national characteristics as such: 'We are at home in Europe' (Robert Wistrich, as cited).

disputes.question: How many Jews came in the First Aliyah, and how many stayed?

positions.view: From 25,000 (Jewish Agency figure) to 60,000 in total (Anita Shapira, 2012), with Shapira estimating that 50–70% later left.

disputes.question: Jewish population of Palestine at the end of the period

positions.view: About 50,000 by 1903 (Barın); about 55,000 at the period's close (reference summary, uncited).
80,000 by 1907 (Elia, 1971, as cited).

entries.topic: The Suez Canal shares, 1875–1876: the loan and the stated reason

claims.text: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, was owned by French financiers and the Khedive of Egypt; by 1874 four-fifths of its trade was British.
Disraeli learned on 15 November 1875 that the Khedive meant to sell his shares and concluded the purchase on 25 November 1875, acquiring 44% of the company's shares for £4,000,000.

Because Parliament was not sitting, the money was advanced by N M Rothschild & Sons under Lionel de Rothschild; the Rothschild Archive calls it a 'technically unsecured loan' and says it was repaid within five months.
William Gladstone attacked the purchase for its 'lack of reference or consent from Parliament'; France remained the majority shareholder.

In the Commons debate of 14 and 21 February 1876 Disraeli defended the purchase 'as a political transaction, and one which I believe is calculated to strengthen the Empire', which 'secures to us a highway to our Indian Empire', and said he did not recommend it 'as a financial investment'.

In the same speech Disraeli said that after the first £1,000,000 a further £2,000,000 'might be demanded in gold the next day', and rejected critics' claim that the Rothschild commission amounted to 15 per cent interest.
Parliament approved the purchase on 21 February 1876.

disputes.question: What did the Rothschild advance cost the Treasury?

positions.view: Critics in Parliament said the commission amounted to 15 per cent.
Disraeli denied that the commission had 'anything to do with the interest on the advance'. None of the sources fetched states the actual commission rate.
